cards.html: This skill covers integration, the reverse of differentiation: antiderivatives, the rules for finding them, and definite integrals as areas under curves. In economics it turns marginal values back into totals.

If F′(x) = f(x), then F is an antiderivative of f. Integration asks: "which function has this derivative?"

∫ 2x dx = x² + C

The constant of integration C is there because constants vanish when you differentiate: x² + 5 and x² − 3 both have derivative 2x. ∫ is a long S (for "sum"), and dx says x is the variable.

Each rule is a derivative rule run backwards.

The power rule backwards: raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.

∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + C
∫ (6x² - 4x + 5) dx
  = 2x³ - 2x² + 5x + C
∫ √x dx = ∫ x^(1/2) dx
        = (2/3) x^(3/2) + C
∫ 3/x² dx = ∫ 3x⁻² dx
          = -3x⁻¹ + C = -3/x + C

Check any integral by differentiating your answer.

If you know marginal cost, integrate to get total cost. The constant C is then the fixed cost, found from extra information.

MC = 3q² - 10q + 40
C(q) = q³ - 5q² + 40q + F
fixed cost 200 -> F = 200
C(q) = q³ - 5q² + 40q + 200

The same works for revenue from marginal revenue (R(0) = 0, so the constant is 0) and for capital stock from investment.

The definite integral from a to b gives a number:

  b
∫  f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
  a

This is the fundamental theorem of calculus. Find any antiderivative F, then subtract its value at the bottom limit from its value at the top. The constant C cancels, so leave it out.

∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx
= [x²] from 1 to 3
= 9 - 1 = 8

Meaning: when f is positive, the definite integral is the area under the curve between a and b. (Area below the x-axis counts as negative.)

And it adds up changes: the integral of a rate of change over a period is the total change. The integral of MC from q = 10 to q = 20 is the extra cost of raising output from 10 to 20.

MC = 4 + 0.2q
∫ from 10 to 20 of (4 + 0.2q) dq
= [4q + 0.1q²] from 10 to 20
= (80 + 40) - (40 + 10) = 70

1. ∫ (5x⁴ + 2x) dx
  2. ∫ (x² − 3x + 7) dx
  3. ∫ (4/x) dx
  4. ∫ e^(2x) dx
  5. ∫ x^(−1/2) dx
  6. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of (3x² + 1) dx.
  7. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to e of (1/x) dx.
  8. MC = 6q + 8 and fixed cost is 50. Find C(q) and C(10).
  9. MR = 100 − 4q. Find total revenue R(q). (R(0) = 0.)
  10. Investment flows in at I(t) = 3√t billion a year. How much capital is added from t = 0 to t = 4?

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

1: x⁵ + x² + C. 2: x³/3 − 3x²/2 + 7x + C. 3: 4 ln x + C. 4: e^(2x)/2 + C. 5: 2√x + C. 6: [x³ + x] = 8 + 2 = 10. 7: ln e − ln 1 = 1. 8: C = 3q² + 8q + 50; C(10) = 430. 9: 100q − 2q². 10: [2t^(3/2)] from 0 to 4 = 16 billion.

quiz.why: Raise the power, divide by the new power.
The power rule fails for n = −1; ln x fills the gap.

quiz.q: MC = 4q + 5 and fixed cost 30. Total cost C(q) = ?
quiz.why: Integrate, then the constant is the fixed cost.

quiz.q: A definite integral needs the constant of integration C.
quiz.why: Myth. C cancels when you subtract F(a) from F(b).

concept.why: 3x² is the derivative. Integrating goes the other way: x⁴/4 + C.

concept.q: ∫₀² f(x) dx is an area, so it can never be negative.
concept.why: Myth. It's a signed area: parts below the x-axis count as negative. ∫₀² (−1) dx = −2.

concept.q: Why do you add + C to an indefinite integral?
o: Every constant has derivative 0, so many functions share the same derivative
It's only there to look neat
concept.why: x² + 1, x² − 7 and x² all have derivative 2x. + C covers all of them.
The antiderivative is x². From 1 to 3: 9 − 1 = 8.

concept.q: ∫₀¹ f·g dx = (∫₀¹ f dx) · (∫₀¹ g dx)
concept.why: Almost always false. With f = g = x: ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3, but (1/2)·(1/2) = 1/4. It works by luck for constants.
